utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow what I'm saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody. Yes, I can follow and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, David Cunningham and Barbara Baruch, along with Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujanic. Could you please repeat the same solemn declaration you made yesterday, to speak the truth, the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take a seat, please. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Nicholls: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on, I want to just clarify one point from yesterday. Early on yesterday we were talking about the problems, the ethnic tensions which were arising in 1991 and you spoke about a rally, this is on page 53 of the transcript, in Prnjavor and you said: In Prnjavor there was a rally which was held by this guy, Zelenbaba, and he said sell your cow, Buy yourself a weapon and they were singing ethnic songs and one could hear them over the loudspeakers. Could you tell us who Zelenbaba was and what his ethnicity was, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zelenbaba was a Serb. I think that he was from Croatia, from the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say ethnic songs they were singing, can you explain what you mean by that, whether there is -- what your meaning is that they were singing ethnic songs at this rally, the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in fact singing Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we talked also yesterday about the mosque in Puraci which you saw blown up and also the mosque in the centre of Lisnja which you saw burning. Did you ever hear anybody take responsibility or did you ever hear who blew up and set fire to those two mosques?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from other people that allegedly Veljko Milankovic said: "I destroyed them and I will build them anew."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so just to be clear, you didn't personally hear Veljko Milankovic say that, you heard that from other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, say, some 10 to 15 days later. That's when I heard it. I was at the camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you hear it from, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but we were imprisoned and we talked among each other, or when our families came, women and children, to bring food to us, then we would talk to them and that's how we heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back, I just want to run through now the rest of the period from your release from the sawmill, what happened after that, until you eventually came to leave Prnjavor in December of 1992. You were released from the sawmill at noon after having been held there overnight and you went into Lisnja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did all of the population of Lisnja, which had been held at the sawmill, return to Lisnja or did some of them go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some went to the camp. They first came to the culture centre in Prnjavor and then the following day, they were transferred to another place, and then the rest returned back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the camp," which camp are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sloga in Prnjavor, the shoe factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you can tell me approximately what per cent of the population returned to Lisnja and what per cent was taken to the Dom and then to Sloga?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 300 people went to Prnjavor and the rest returned back. Some stayed with neighbours in Prnjavor and some people had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that some people were taken to the Dom, went to the Dom, did they go there of their own free will or were they taken there as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which people were there -- taken there? Were these men and women and children or which part of the population?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were males aged 14 up to 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what personally happened to you? You said that you were released, after your release you went into town. Were you taken back into custody at any point after that? After your release from the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later on, they released us to go home, and then sometime in the afternoon, around 3.00 or 4.00, my neighbour -- I fell asleep and my neighbour woke me up. She said get up, there is shooting all over. And then we escaped to Konjuhovci. We stayed in various houses. I stayed there for several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who was shooting? Could you hear the shooting? Did you see the shooting?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a distance, I saw troops. They had what we call SNB, olive-drab uniforms. I also saw troops in camouflage uniforms shooting and we simply had to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everybody flee the village again at this point?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some remained there, hiding in houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Konjuhovci?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Why did you leave Konjuhovci? Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to Lisnja again, since I had livestock there. Somebody had to take care of it. When I returned, we were told we had to go to Prnjavor to surrender or else we would face problems with police again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who told you this? Who made this announcement to you and to the other people in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho Mujanic, who attended negotiations. Then the criminal police came to our village. They had a list of people who had to report to the police station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on that list?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this time, up to this point, when were you told to report to the police station in Prnjavor, in between that point and the time, the few days, when you'd been released from the sawmill, was there any resistance that you saw from the Muslim population in Lisnja during those few days?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go to the police station in Prnjavor? Did you obey that order?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to obey it. Because of others, there were many women, children, the elderly there. So we had to do as we were told or else children would suffer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -- how did you get to the police station in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a tractor. I drove the tractor to Prnjavor and then I left it with a neighbour in front of his yard. There were many people in the tractor-trailer. In fact it was full with people. We went to the police station and from there, we were taken to the Sloga shoe factory in buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We will talk about the Sloga in a minute. But if you know, if you saw it, how many names were on this list of people who had to report to the Prnjavor police station?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 32, 32 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was a young 14 year old with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the police station before you were transported to the Sloga factory?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, in the hallway, we saw two soldiers; they had the SAO Krajina insignia on their shoulders. They insulted us, cursed us, and then they put us in another room, the police did, and there were interrogations going on there; and after that we were transferred to Sloga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there already men in custody in the police station when you arrived there, or were the only people detained there the group that you arrived with?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 32 of us there. We were taken to a room for interrogation. We waited there for three hours. Whereas, in the prison, in the solitary confinement cells, there were, I don't know exactly how many people, but definitely not less than 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And when you said "prison," are you talking -- and these confinement cells, are you talking about these cells at the police station or is that a different detention facility?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cells of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you told by -- were you personally interrogated?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did interrogate me but only upon my arrival at the Sloga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how long were you and these other men held at the police station before you were taken to Sloga?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept us there for three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At any time were you told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say anything to us. They didn't explain why we were there. They simply said that they would put several questions to us and then release us to go home but that's not what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they put you on the bus, did you know where the bus was going, where you were going to be taken?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of escort for the bus to prevent people from trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, tell me, tell us, if you can, what happened when you arrived at the Sloga factory. How far away is that, first of all, from the Prnjavor police station?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 700 metres, perhaps one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened upon your arrival at the Sloga factory?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got off the bus. Then they opened up another building and put us there. There were already people in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness P1796.6, please. That's a photograph. This photo was shown to the witness last Sunday before his testimony. We have a copy here if it's easier. Can you take a look at that photo, sir - if it's easier you can look at it to your right rather than on the monitor - and tell me if you recognise that building.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Sloga shoe factory and the shot is taken from the other side, because the entrance is on another side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is that a fair and accurate representation of the way that it looked when you arrived there in 1992 or is there anything particularly different?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this side here. I didn't. And then the other side, the other side is where we entered the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you know from living there -- so you didn't see this view of the Sloga factory at the time you were taken there for detention, but you recognise it from seeing it on other occasions? Is that right? Just so I understand you.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry to have interrupted you with that photo. Can you tell us now about what happened, you started to, when you arrived at the Sloga factory, what happened to you and the other men, how you were processed into that factory, the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got off the bus, they opened up the door, there had already been some 100 people sitting in there, and they put us into that room as well; and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who put you into the room? Who were the guards at the Sloga factory?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were policemen and they, the policemen, put us into that one room. They locked us in and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And there were about 100 men in that room when you arrived. Your group was put in there so your first day in the Sloga factory, you were in a room with about 130 other men; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe the room to the Chamber, please. What was in the room and how big was the room?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I couldn't give you the exact square area but let's say 10 by 12 metres approximately. There was nothing inside. That room was vacant when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you just describe it, say, in comparison to this courtroom we are in now, how much bigger or smaller it was if that helps you rather than talking in numbers.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something like this, perhaps a bit larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And there was nothing inside the room. Do you mean that literally, that this was just a completely square, empty room without any chairs, tables, nothing?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two tables by the window and there was cardboard on the floor on which we slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long were you held in the Sloga factory before you were eventually released?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was imprisoned for 36 days. I had to pay to get released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And we will talk about your release. I want you now to tell us about what those 36 days were like for you before you were released and what the conditions there were. First of all, what was the age range of the prisoners in the room you were in? What was the youngest, what was the oldest man?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say from 14 to 60 years old. The youngest one was 14, the oldest was 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity or religion of all the people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detained in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these civilians or soldiers, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know many of these people? Were they neighbours? Friends?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were neighbours, friends, relatives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell me about what you were given to eat while you were at the Sloga factory. What kind of food was provided to you and by whom?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get any food from police. Sometimes police would allow the villagers, women and children, to bring us some food, and that was the only time we ate. When they want to let them in they would come in, bring us food, and that was when we ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, I think you told us, had seeing the way things were going, had sent your family abroad earlier. Was there anybody to bring you food? Did you have any relatives or friends who could bring food specifically for you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have anybody there, but for example my neighbour was there with me, so whenever his son came to bring him food, he would share his food with me or perhaps somebody else would share their piece of bread with me and that's when I ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were family members or citizens allowed to bring food in? Could they bring it in, whenever, seven days a week or as often as they liked or was that restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were allowed to come at 10.00 every day except on occasions when some of the policemen who were guarding us there were -- had lost some of their relatives on the battle front. Then they would lock us in. We had to keep quiet, not speak with anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you adequately, I'm talking about you personally, provided with food? Was there enough for to you eat, having other people you know share their food with you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have enough, but I had enough to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose any weight while you were held there for those 36 days?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I lost a lot of weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about water? Can you describe whether there was -- adequate water was provided to you for drinking?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was water but it was not always accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your clothing? You were there for over a month. Were you able to wash your clothes or have new clothes brought in or were you given any clothes? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the clothes that I came in were the clothes that I left in. There was no way for me to wash my clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And let's talk about the space in the room. When you first arrived, was there enough space for everybody to be comfortable when -- during the day or when sleeping?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we did not have enough room. We slept in the sitting position, but later on, they opened up another room which was a bit bigger. There were about 370 of us in that room but people would leave and some new people would arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So initially there wasn't even enough room for everybody to lie down at the same time but later on, that got better; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They opened up the second room so we split the -- all of us split between these two rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was it before the second room was opened?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You started talking about the numbers of people there, people coming and going. Could you -- I know the numbers -- well, did the numbers of people detained there fluctuate while you were there for those 36 days?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Children were released, for example, and they started releasing children after six or seven days, after interrogation, but the number didn't change because some were released but at the same time other people were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what do you think, best -- I know you don't know exactly, but what was the average number of people being detained there on any given day during the 36 days you were there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the youngest was 14, the oldest was 60.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I was clear. What I mean is: How many men were detained there because there were 132 at one point and I think you said 387 later. How many prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On an average.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 377 altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said there was cardboard on the floor and you slept on that. Were you provided with any other sleeping facilities?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have anything else. There was not enough cardboard for everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the floor made up that was under the cardboard, if somebody did have a piece of cardboard to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any medical care provided to prisoners while you were there? In other words, if somebody needed a prescription or was ill or wounded, did anybody see a doctor while they were there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He needs to clarify this because obviously it makes a difference if there were inmates that needed medical attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if there was no one who needed medical attention. So I suppose -- have you followed -- have you understood what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In order to be able to tell us yes or no, you need to know in the first place whether at any given time during those 36 days that you were there anyone needed medical attention, asked for it, and was given or refused medical attention. So I would suggest you start from there. And my first question to you is: During those 36 days, as far as you are aware, did anyone need and ask for medical attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had a toothache and no medical assistance was given to me, and the explanation was that there was no water in town and I could not have my tooth extracted. And there was another person whose name was Zoran, he beat up one of us on the head and I saw that that person's head was dressed. That's what I saw on the following morning. And this person's name was Alija. On the following morning, this person was taken away and that was after I had seen his head being dressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would assume from your answer that while you were not given the treatment that you asked for or the attention, medical attention that you asked for, this other person that was wounded in the head was given medical attention, at least before being removed away from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say for a fact that he was seen by a doctor. All I can say is that in the morning his wounds were dressed. I slept in another room, so I don't know what was going on during the night, nor did I hear anything during the night or the previous evening. All I could see was that in the morning his head was dressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from your case and this gentleman's case, are you aware of any other instances when inmates that were in your room or in any of the other rooms in the Sloga factory asked for medical attention or needed medical attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Nobody else asked to be seen by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were interrogated once you got to the Sloga. Can you tell us about that. When were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an office and a policeman would take us there. His name was Drago Kalabic. He was the one who interrogated us. There were more than one of them but there was one person called Petrovic, but I was interrogated by this guy Drago Kalabic and we would stay in that office for an hour or two hours. We would be interrogated for an hour or two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you interrogated? How many times?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice a day. Not all of us, but some of us would be taken into that office twice a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But personally, how many times in total, while you were held there the 36 days, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can tell me how many times you were interrogated while you were held there the 36 days? How many times were you personally interrogated? 10? 20? 2?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken for interrogation on two days twice every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And finally we had an agreement for me to give him some money in order to be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that. What kind of questions were you asked during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions were: Are you loyal to the Serbian government? Why do you have weapons? Why do you want to rebel -- although nobody was rebelling. Why are you bothered by all this? And things like that. Some of these questions didn't really make too much sense to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these interrogations were you ever told specifically why you were there? Were you ever charged with a crime? Were you ever told what you had done to deserve this?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that allegedly I had not surrendered the machine gun of the Territorial Defence; however, I wanted to be confronted with Captain Nedjo. Later on, I saw Captain Nedjo and I asked him why he didn't tell them that I had handed over the weapon. His response was that he did give a statement saying that I had handed over the machine gun, and he also said that he didn't know why I was being kept here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you ever interrogated anybody -- anywhere during those 36 days other than in a part of the factory? In other words, were you ever taken to the SUP or anywhere else and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me but there were people who were taken to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You talked about one man who was injured in a beating and that later on you saw that he'd had some dressing put on his wounds. Did you -- were people beaten in the Sloga factory, other than that one incident you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not beaten there but people who were brought from the MUP, they were all black and blue, and they had bruises and cuts on their face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that after returning from interrogation?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask whether any of those people who were bruised and bleeding returning from their interrogation, did you see whether they were bandaged ever?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not bandaged because they mostly had internal bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, other than the police who guarded -- you said were guarding the factory, anybody else -- did any other officials or other persons come into the factory to interrogate people or do anything else with the prisoners in the factory? Anybody else come in from the outside world?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On weekends, soldiers would come from the front line and they would shoot near the Sloga factory. Sometimes they would even arrive with dies on their faces, with arms, and then they would come in, threatening to kill us and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did that occur?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weekends were the worst times, that is Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, you may have answered this, I don't think so, while you were there, did you know how long you would be detained? Did anybody ever tell you, you're here for 36 days or you're here for about a month or did you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have -- we didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained at the Sloga factory, did you do any kind of work? Were you forced to work, either at the factory or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would collect garbage in the town, and then when there was -- there were exchanges of dead bodies in Derventa, there were 20 bodies in one pit. Then we excavated them, we had to put them in boxes, and to prepare them for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who guarded you when you were on these work details during your detention?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this just to be clear was this work voluntary or was it something that you had no choice but to do?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't have a choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, please, how you came to be released from the Sloga factory?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Kalabic asked me to come for interrogation. He said: "I understand you're alone." He inquired where my children and wife were. I said they were in Germany. He says: "Why aren't you in Germany?" I told him: "Well, I'm here, aren't I?" And he says: "Okay, I can help you get released, but I am building my house and I need some money." And that's how he released me, on the following day I brought 300 German marks to him. Altogether, I gave him about 600 or 700 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his official position, if you know? Dragan Kalabic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman in the crime department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just let me see if I understand you. Was the release from what you said on the understanding that you were going to go join your family in Germany if you were released? Is that what you -- what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he released me. He asked me to give him money. On every day at 8.00, we had a call-up, and every day I would give him some money, and then on one day he told me: "I can't keep you here. You have to run away." I ran away. I found a bus driver. I gave him 1600 German marks to give me a ride across the border. I was in the toilet all the time. And that's how I crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this policeman told you the time had come for you to leave; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after you were released from the Sloga factory was it that you left Prnjavor hiding in this bus?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had work obligation for three or four more months. I can't say exactly. We were felling trees in the forest, and we had to drive logs to the fighters' home. There were some people who also worked on the fish farm there, cleaning the ponds and then ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I'm just curious, was the Sloga factory guarded day and night or left unguarded? Could you walk in and out of the place without difficulty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was guarded by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How could you escape without being noticed or stopped or even shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very difficult to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But was it made easy for you to escape? Because it seems that when you were told now it's time to go, you just escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I can clear -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was released. I was released. Every day we had a call-up. In the village, everybody had to go into the village to be present during the call-up, in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's how -- okay this needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You paid these 600 or 700 marks to the policeman, Kalabic, to get you released from the Sloga factory?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your release, you stayed in Lisnja until approximately December 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, where were you living, between your release and when you finally left Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my brother's house because my house had burnt down, and I was in my brother's house all the time up to the 20th of December, 1992, and I had work obligation. Every morning at 6.00, we had to be down there, and there was a man from the military department who recorded our presence; and then we did not have to report to -- for call-ups at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was the work obligation, was that -- how many days a week did you have to do this work obligation?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, without any breaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can just -- you started to but just tell us what kind of work obligation you personally were required to perform, what kind of jobs, once you'd been released from the Sloga factory.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to do the felling, chopping woods, and if the area was not accessible to a tractor, then we had to form a line and we had to physically carry the logs down to the village from the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever work on any property owned by Veljko Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While we were still in the camp, we were cleaning the road that leads up to his house on Vucjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then just to be very clear, the policeman who told you that you ought to leave Lisnja or Prnjavor and join your family, was that the same policeman that you had paid money to in order to be released from the Sloga factory? Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you left and you were hiding in this bus which took you away, what property were you able to bring with you? How much of your property from your former life in Lisnja were you able to bring with you when you left?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I had just one jacket. Everything else had burned down. I had a jacket, a T-shirt, a pair of shoes, and those were the things that I had on when I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to sign any documents forfeiting your property, homes, other property, in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not, because I escaped with the help of Drago. That was the arrangement. He helped me to leave Prnjavor. I was supposed to wait by the fish pond for the arrival of that bus that was on its way to Munich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said personally, you did not. Did other people have to sign such documents forfeiting or transferring their property?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I don't know. We've heard enough about this from at least 50, 60 other witnesses. Do you need reconfirmation from this witness that didn't have to sign one himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this is my last question. His cousin had to sign these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then ask him whether he knows of anyone who had to sign them and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody from your family have to sign documents leaving their property in order to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was Naim Mujanic, my relative, who signed a document forfeiting all of his property to the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Before we proceed with the cross-examination, Mr. Cunningham, do you have any further communications from Mr. Ackerman regarding the Bosanski Petrovac list of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Mr. Ackerman has advised me that he wishes to stand by those objections and asks the Court to rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's hand down the decision before we proceed any further on this matter. The Trial Chamber has seen the Prosecution -- the Defence objection to the OTP proposed exhibits, list of which appears attached to the objection itself. The Trial Chamber in the first place refers to Exhibits P1818, P1820, P1821, P1822, and reserves its judgement, its decision, after having heard evidence from the Prosecution identifying the source of each of these four documents. The decision of this Trial Chamber is also reserved with regard to P1832, after hearing further submissions from the parties. As to the remaining documents, they are all being admitted with the understanding that the probative value of each and every one of them will be determined at the right stage, together, and with other documents, and taken into consideration all the circumstances of the case. And this is in line with previous decisions of this Trial Chamber, particularly those taken in the initial period of this trial, between admissibility and tenderability and probative value of documents at this stage of the trial. Thank you. Yes. Now, Mr. Mujanic, it's the turn of the Defence now to cross-examine you. I'm just going to remind you of the words I told you yesterday. You have an obligation towards both parties here to answer truthfully and fully each question that is put to you, irrespective of where it's coming from. The fact that it's coming from the Defence does not mean anything, it should not mean anything to you. Your duty is to answer each and every question. Madam Baruch will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Cross-examined by Ms. Baruch:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujanic.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Barbara Baruch and I represent the accused in this case, Mr. Brdjanin. The first thing I'd like to talk to you about is statements that you have previously given before you came into this Tribunal, and I have seen one written statement that was signed by you, and it was dated October 21st and 22nd of 1991. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2001. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Madam Baruch -- usher, please, could you hand him a copy of his statement? I think you need to get that from the Prosecution and not from the Registrar because it's not an exhibit. You need to show him the English version too because that's the one we are mostly interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving that statement, Mr. Mujanic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't -- are your initials on the B/C/S version? Did you initial it or sign the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because I look at the English version, not being familiar with your language. Did you get a copy of that statement after you gave it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you given any other statements, any other written statements, besides that one?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave once in Germany a statement, and twice in Bosnia, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to clarify about the statements. I don't think the witness signed a B/C/S copy of his statement. When we take statements, they are generated in English, it's read back by a translator. The witness agrees that what was read back is accurate. They sign that. Later on, we can't do a simultaneous translation, the statement is translated from English into B/C/S, the witness doesn't sign that copy. They only sign one copy which is the English original.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, that that's what was told me today, but that directly contradicts what the witness says or at least my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get down -- give me a copy of the B/C/S version and we cut it short because there is either his initials on it or not. And it's as simple as that. Yes, let me see it. But on the English version we always have it but we don't even get the -- show it to the witness. Ask him whether he sees his initials there and then he would need to tell us why, before he said that he initialed also the B/C/S version or whether it was a misunderstanding or a mistake on his part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand that. I know that I signed the statements that I gave but not in Bosnian language but rather in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Chapter closed. Next?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, if you don't understand my questions, would you please just indicate in some manner to me and I will try to make them clearer. Okay? Thank you. Now, you also said that you gave a written statement in Germany? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give that statement -- did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it, yes. There was an interpreter there in Germany, and I signed that statement but I don't remember what language it was in, the statement was also read out to me and then I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to keep a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive copies in Germany, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that statement also concern the same events that you talked about here in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom did you give that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. That was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a man there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it was a German man or a Bosnian man?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a German.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How did you get to know to go to give that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived as a refugee in Germany. I worked there, and I don't know how it happened but police came to my apartment once to tell me that I should report for an interview. And I came there and saw that there was an interpreter there and then I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also told me that twice in Sanski Most you gave a statement. Is that the same statement you have in front of you when you said twice in Sanski Most, or was that a different occasion?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we didn't finish on the first day, we completed on the second day, regarding that statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's why I asked you the question, because I noticed in the copy of the October 21st and 22nd 2001 statement it actually says two different dates. So when you said you gave two statements in Sanski Most, is it what you have in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement on the one day, and on the second day. We had to do it during two days because we couldn't complete it all in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me intervene because I don't think he's following what you're asking. You mentioned earlier -- what Mrs. Baruch is asking you is precisely whether this statement that you say you gave on two consecutive days in Sanski Most is the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal or whether it's some other statement to some other authorities that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is this statement, the one that I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's because earlier on, you said, when you were asked whether you had given other statements, you said that you had given a statement in Germany and also in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was twice, or rather over two days. We didn't manage to complete it in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you don't or weren't living in Sanski Most at the time but you were asked to go there to give your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that to anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. We'll see. Wait, it's too early for me to stop Mrs. Baruch asking this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I gave a statement in Sanski Most, in the village of Tomina; that's where I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who asked you to go there to give your statement.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to my house. I can't remember their names but two women came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they people from the Office of the Prosecutor, one of them, and one an interpreter or was it an official from Bosnia who came to your house?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an official from the Prosecution and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the statement wasn't given at your house, it was given at Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm understanding now, that you actually gave your statement in the place that you live to people who came to your house, so you did not have to go to them, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave it in my house because I had no means of transportation to go to Sanski Most, and the weather was quite bad. I also had to work at the time and that is why we did this over the duration of two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And before you gave your statement, did you talk about what your statement would involve with anybody? I'm not talking about the same day, to those women. I'm talking about before the date that you gave your statement.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that at all. Nobody instructed me what to say. I know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Mujanic, at any time has anybody talked to you about how you should testify or what things you should emphasise to this Court?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need anybody's assistance regarding that. I know what had happened and if somebody asks me I will tell them about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There came a time when you spoke with Mr. Nicholls, I believe, the Prosecutor who has been questioning you before me, and you spoke with him before you came to this Court, is that correct, before you came in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply recollected -- I didn't need to refresh my memory but we simply went over my statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You went over this one statement that you have in front of you or did you also go over your German statement?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He put questions to me, I answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, we have no German statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, when you were talking with Mr. Nicholls before coming to this courtroom, were you shown any documents, pictures, videotapes, or statements by anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this statement in Bosnian. I've read it. Questions were put to me. I answered them. And that was all. And then I also saw photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So just so that I understand and the Court understands, the only thing that you saw before coming to this court when you were talking with Mr. Nicholls is photographs and your own statement; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because yesterday, Mr. Nicholls had you looking at a report, a military report, and I'm wondering if you saw that before you came into this courtroom. Have you ever seen that before?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it two days ago?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were talking privately with Mr. Nicholls; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've said something about the fact that you were not interested in politics, and I'd like to know if at any time you've been a member of any political party, not merely back in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. I wasn't involved in that. I had other things to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it that you never were a member of the Communist Party? That would be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were agreeing with me, correct me if I'm wrong, and I take it that you were never a member, never not even today, a member of the SDA? Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, you were agreeing with me as well. Have you reviewed the information that you would be giving with any authority from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's actually answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: Have you reviewed what your testimony would be, what you knew, with any authority from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday there was a map that had a legend on it that Mr. Nicholls used and I thought that Mr. Cunningham had taken it home. Mr. Cunningham believes that I took it home. I don't have it and I'm wondering if I could just see it for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Ackerman has it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: He's easy to blame. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Really, if the witness could look at it on the ELMO, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm wondering if you have seen that map before yesterday, Mr. Mujanic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The reason that I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have seen it but I'm not entirely sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason that I ask you that, and maybe you can make it clear to me, that somebody has gone through that map and made a legend, we call it, and colours, to indicate the ethnicity of various villages. But when you were testifying, I think it's the village called Galjupovci, it's hard for me to read, which is designated by the legend as being a Muslim village and I think you told me that was -- us that it was a mixed village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serbs there, Croats. It's a mixed population village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I just wanted to know or to make certain that although you were vouching for the correctness of the names of the villages, you really had nothing to do with designating the ethnicity on those maps -- that map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't see Vucjak on that map, and the reason I think I don't see it is perhaps it's too small. Do you know where Vucjak is and is it on that map?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't see that. No. You can't see it on the map. It's -- there is a road leading to Derventa and then from that main road, there is a road going to the right towards Doboj and Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is that the place where you were working on Veljko Milankovic's property that you talked about during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We built -- we worked on building the road towards his house, and then another group came to do the same thing, to perform the same work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was while you were staying at -- detained at Sloga; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you really know the ownership of the property that you worked on or you're just associating it with Mr. Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who guarded us there talked about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talked about the property being owned by Mr. Milankovic or controlled by him? Which?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his house, that his mother allegedly was born there, and we went to clear that road because it was all badly neglected so that was the road leading to the house where he was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm understanding that now. And you told us at the beginning that you had a pretty successful business, at least it sounded like that to me, with 50 employees. That was disturbed by the war in Croatia. Was it a very successful business?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My brother and I worked as partners. We were the owners of the company, we worked together. We had our own saws and the business was very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told the Tribunal, Mr. Mujanic, that you had 50 employees. Were those 50 full-time employees?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only -- we hired them only as needed. We had ten people who worked full time and were fully insured, and then, if needed, we would hire seasonal workers, if we needed to do some extra reforestation and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you for a minute about the ten full time employees. Were they hired at Lisnja village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no work in Lisnja. We worked only in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the ten full-time people, they weren't local people who you knew from Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people were from Lisnja, some people were from Kotor Varos, Siprage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ethnicity of the ten full-time people, were they all Muslim?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two were Serbs. They were from a village in the vicinity of Vrbanjci. So they were Serbs and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of those ten people were people you had to lay off because of the war in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to. How else would I be able to pay for them? We -- there was a lot of work that we had completed but were unable to collect money for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm understanding how difficult it was during wartime and a period of conflict to continue a business, Mr. Mujanic. I don't want you to think that I'm not. And I'm wondering if you noticed in Prnjavor itself that established businesses were also having difficulty, continued to keep -- continuing to keep all of their employees employed during 1991 and 1992? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rarely went to Prnjavor. I know that people were laid off, those of non-Serb ethnicity. There were several neighbours of mine who were laid off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were most of your friends and all of your relatives non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Muslims, my neighbours, for example, Hasan Zukandzic, also used to work in Metalic [phoen] and was fired. Not only him but Edib Mujanic, who was a teacher, he was also fired. Huso Korkaric was director or rather mayor of Prnjavor, and was a teacher, he was also fired. So there were a number of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any Serbs who were let go as well?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mujanic, I need to ask you, then, were you friendly with any Serbs whom you would know if they had difficulties with their employment?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're telling this Tribunal then is about the people that you were friendly with and what you knew happened to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about when the relationship between the Serbs and the Bosniaks became tense yesterday, and you started talking about 1992. I think about the time that you sent your wife and children off to Germany, but Mr. Nicholls directed to you tell the Court about a rally in Prnjavor. I think we know that you did not attend the rally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you must have known someone who attended the rally because you've told us about the rally, including the types of songs that were sung there. So who told you about that rally?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My neighbours told me about that, people who were there in Prnjavor. There was a place near my house called Jure, and this is where we talked about that. A colleague of mine said: I had been to Prnjavor and he told me about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here. We will have a 25-minute break and resume immediately thereafter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one preliminary, Your Honour, briefly. We may have to move some witnesses around next week. I've asked counsel if the next scheduled witness is going to start today, and we don't know. The next witness, if he only has tomorrow, will likely go into Monday. We didn't foresee that, which I'm just trying to let the Court know. We may have to move the scheduled Monday witness in order to continue and keep the Tuesday witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long did you anticipate your examination-in-chief to last with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: With the next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've only got tomorrow -- if he starts tomorrow, we've only got tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Longer than that for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need more than one sitting for --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll have to check with Ms. Korner, but I think in total she said he will definitely not be done with his testimony tomorrow, if he doesn't start until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then my answer is obvious, I mean you will need to reschedule the list of witnesses for next week for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just trying to give the Court some notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing I can do is I can limit your examination-in-chief for just tomorrow's sitting, not extendable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We would prefer that you not do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the option I give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll re schedule if we have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to know, therefore, whether we are sitting tomorrow as suggested yesterday, morning right through 4.00 in the afternoon, or whether it's going to be just a morning sitting like today's?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we've agreed to all day on Thursday, tomorrow, as we stated -- as we talked about, and the next witness will take all day tomorrow in chief, if he starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I will tell you that I promise the Court, and I will keep my word, that Thursday we will go the whole day. But yesterday, I thought I had arranged through Mr. Lawrence that I can speak with my client for one half afterwards but apparently the scheduling of bringing prisoners is not subject to the Court and so I had to wait and then go to detention and then come back and then start work. I didn't go to sleep until 10.30 last night and I'm wiped out and that was with working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't look it, Madam Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. And I'll keep that in mind. But that was with working half a day. So I will keep my word about Thursday but I have very severe feelings that it's totally impossible for me to keep in touch with my client and communicate with him or any of the lawyers, and also to be prepared when they come to court. So I have indicated that to Mr. Nicholls as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't single yourself out, Mrs. Baruch, because until quite recently, that's how it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sittings used to start at 9.30 in the morning and finish at 4.30 or 5.00 in the afternoon. And that's how it went and when it was like that, cases lasted less, shorter period of time. There is a difference of about one hour or one hour and a half per day. So -- anyway, we will take it up. I take it that tomorrow we'll sit right through 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Baruch, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic I hope you can help me by making sure that you understand my questions so that we can both help the Court and make this go as quickly as possible, okay? That's my intention. Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry I forgot to ask you the town in Germany where you gave your statement. Could I just have the name of that town?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kirhajm Tek near Stuttgart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the police station there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you started telling me about a colleague, a friend of yours, who lived I think in Urije and you talked about the rally in Prnjavor from 1991. Can you tell me the name of that colleague, please?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Edib Mujanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people there who had that discussion with the both of you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some ten of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So ten people came and had a discussion about what the one colleague had heard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you talk about that event, please?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a story of how things were going in Prnjavor, because I personally didn't go to Prnjavor, not just ask me, people avoided going Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there because there were drunken soldiers or reservists roaming around so all of us avoided going there. We relied on the stories told by people who did go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct that you just generally know about the music at the rally? You don't really know which particular songs were played or what in particular was said? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that my colleague had told me about the Chetnik songs and he also quoted Zelenbaba saying that every Serb should sell their cow and buy a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your colleague attended that rally? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was there. Not at the rally. He just stopped by the Hotel Nacional where that rally was taking place in front of the department store. He was passing by and he stopped to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he stopped for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Baruch, let's proceed. I mean, I won't allow you to go into such minute details which have little or no relevance. I mean it's -- go ahead with the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He stopped enough to be able to tell the witness the words which he told him and that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we talk about Mr. Milankovic, Mr. Mujanic, for a few minutes? How many times have you personally seen him?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him before the developments in Lisnja on that day, and then I heard somebody saying: "This is the guy called Milankovic." And that's when I saw him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And my question was: How many times have you seen him personally?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him on that day and I believe that I saw him once again when we went to Prnjavor by tractor. We were passing by a bus stop, and I believe that his -- he was wearing plaster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is that a bandage of some sort, plaster?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't that close. I didn't dare look straight into his eyes, but I threw a glance and I believe that it was a bandage of some sort or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are the only two occasions on which you've seen Mr. Milankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I may have seen him later on but I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I've written down that you say you saw him at the sawmill, you saw him casually just an averted glance when you were in Prnjavor, and those are the two occasions that you have told me you remember, correct? That you remember now.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm wondering if he came to the Sloga detention facility on an occasion when he spoke with all of the people there and told you there that you shouldn't worry but that you would be safe, you wouldn't be hurt. Does that refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I saw him once again when we were working close to his house, when we were clearing the road. That was another time when I saw him. I don't remember him saying that nothing would happen to us. That is something I can't recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Sloga, how about do you recollect him being at Sloga at all and speaking with all of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him at Sloga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm just trying to see what you recall. I assume you're not saying he never came there, you just don't remember such an incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he ever came there.
