utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's your recollection. Back in 2001, when you gave a statement, you said that when you were doing forced labour in the birth village of Mr. Milankovic, he came, he told us that he had blown up the mosques in Lisnja and he said he was sorry that he had to destroy that. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Milankovic had said that he had destroyed the mosque and that he himself would rebuild it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because I'm looking at the language --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we should follow our practice. Give him a copy of his statement in his language if she is going to refresh his memory with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think he has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Do you still have the copy of your statement, Mr. Mujanic? Can I have a copy of it in the Serb -- B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I've been told that the Court is far ahead of me in reading B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in the English on page 7 that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to page 8, please. The third paragraph before the last, from the bottom, and it starts "radnu" [B/C/S spoken]. Keep reading it. And the last two sentences, one starting with "rekao" [B/C/S spoken], et cetera, he said he was sorry that he had to destroy them. Do you remember saying those words to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now Mr. Mujanic, you remember the incident when he apologised for that? And I think you just told us, Mr. Milankovic said he himself would rebuild that mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now I'd like to go back to the sawmill incident because from reading your statement, I got the impression that Mr. Milankovic was very careful and solicitous of the women, that when they were frightened by what was occurring, he let them go into the restaurant so that they could feel safer. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He allowed them to go into the restaurant. The door had been broken in so the women and the children were allowed to go into the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was by his direct instruction, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The women and children entered the restaurant and that's where they spent the whole night, in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mujanic, the Prosecutor gives us information as they get it, and I have a supplemental information sheet that tells me you indicated to Mr. Nicholls when you spoke with him that when he, Mr. Milankovic, ordered the women and children into the restaurant of the factory or ordered that they be allowed to go in there, he also, Milankovic also said: "Nothing is going to happen to you." Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he did say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you saw Milankovic at the sawmill, was he in a uniform or was he dressed in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him at the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when he was at the sawmill and wearing a uniform, can you describe what the uniform was like? Was it a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the colour of it, please? If you remember?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a multi-coloured uniform, predominantly green but there were other colours as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume, because I've heard, that he had adopted or adopted a certain patch that would have symbol of a wolf on it; is that right? Was that on his uniform as well?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A white wolf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how would you distinguish or can you tell me how that uniform was different from what you described in your statement as a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA uniform was olive-drab, grayish uniform, whereas his uniform was a camouflage, a multi-coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when Mr. Milankovic was up at the sawmill, were there other men in similar uniforms as his, that multi-coloured camouflage uniform with the wolf on it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were others in the same uniform. It was his army, his troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was my question, the question in my mind yesterday. Were all of the troops that you saw there, the troops who were wearing the uniform of Milankovic, with the white wolf symbol on the sleeve?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also police officers there, so not everybody wore that same uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the police officers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you said there were also some troops there at the sawmill from a different town, and maybe somebody can help me. It started with an L, like Laris -- can you help me with that? A unit from a different town.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were troops from Laktasi but they came from a different side. Lisnja was completely encircled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so the Laktasi troops, they were not with you at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lisnja was completely encircled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would have been on the other side of Lisnja from where you were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an officer with them, I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you help me understand this, then, Mr. Mujanic? You were about 2.5 kilometres away from your village, Lisnja, which you could --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- see from where you were? You could see the skyline and perhaps you could see the first buildings, but I think you told us yesterday that you couldn't see maybe the streets or what people were doing inside the village. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no people there, and one could see 60 or even up to 70 per cent of Lisnja. Obviously you couldn't see every street, and you couldn't tell every single house, but you could see a lot of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me here, I'm trying to understand. I know you weren't up -- or were you up very high so that you were looking down at the village from where you were?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were at the foot. The village was a bit higher so you could -- from down there, you could see the entire village which is uphill on a plateau, and you could have a good view of it from down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the troops from Laktasi, could you actually see the troops from Laktasi on the other side of Lisnja from where you were staying at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see them. But at 12.00 when we returned to Lisnja, I saw the troops and later on I learned those were troops from Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm understanding better. And you also said that there were some police officers there, and some JNA officers or soldiers. The JNA soldiers or at least that's how you referred to them in your statement, in the English translation, were they standing with you at the sawmill as well or was there only the Wolves of Vucjak soldiers with Milankovic with you at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an officer there, and there were police officers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the interpretation of your language that I've just been given says there was an officer there, meaning a, one, JNA officer there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was an officer with a higher rank. I don't know where from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- you said he was of higher rank. Did you see insignia, special insignias on his uniform? Is that how you know that, Mr. Mujanic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of stars and stripes. A yellow stripe. And since I served in the army myself, I believe that he was a major. I cannot be sure because the insignia and those stars and stripes changed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think that you indicated -- thank you for that information. But I think you also indicated either in your statement or in your testimony that they were communicating with others, that they were speaking in codes and you could not understand that. Did you watch somebody speak on a radio or walkie-talkie or some instrument?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They carried out conversations using a Motorola. I did not hear what the officer said. I only know that Milankovic asked the officer to bring the multi-rocket launcher and the recoilless gun to that site and that was approved by the officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "to that site," you meant a site at the sawmill or away from the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That place is left, to the sawmill. There is another elevation from which the multi-rocket launcher and the recoilless gun opened fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you told us yesterday there were about 50 men who were in the vicinity of the sawmill, are you talking about 50 Milankovic wolves and police officers?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 50 Milankovic's wolves and there also police officers aligned by the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember about how many police officers there were there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you. There were quite a few of them but how many, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us that you heard Milankovic give the Hodza, who you identified in your statement as a man with the first name Jusuf, some permission to take sometime to go back to Lisnja to try to get some men from Lisnja to come over to the sawmill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all of the first people who went to the sawmill, those were the peaceful people who were obeying the instruction that had come over the loud speaker, "Go up to the saw mill," but there were some people who initially did not go up to the sawmill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were people who had been working in the field and they were not aware of anything. There were also infirm, elderly people, and there were also people -- like I said in my statement, there were some lads, some 30 of them, who collected the weapons without the ammunition, and they had stayed behind and then the Hodza went back to talk them into joining the others at the sawmill and the Hodza was given 30 minutes to do that. That was the deadline. And if he didn't manage to do the task, then the shelling would start. That was -- that was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So just working from what you've just told us, did you actually see yourself the Hodza come back with 30 young men who were bringing weapons with them to the sawmill site? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hodza was returning in his car, and the people were on foot, walking towards the sawmill. They were throwing their weapons into the fields and as they were walking downhill, the troops would be there and they would beat them on the heads and on their backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these men who were throwing weapons down into the fields, did they actually go up to the sawmill or were they diverted to some buses?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were walking downhill, shelling started, and the troops, Milankovic's troop met them, they beat them up, they put them on a bus, and they took them to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you could answer my question, were they diverted directly to the bus so that they didn't get up to the area of the sawmill where you were? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on the left side, and there was a place where wheat was exchanged for flour and that's where the bus was, and as they arrived, they would be loaded on to that bus and finally they were taken to Prnjavor. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was that one bus?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said that the shelling already had started as the Hodza was driving back and the men were walking down the hill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard about those men before from your statement -- strike that. I don't -- I don't want to leave Milankovic for a minute. At any time, did you see Mr. Milankovic drunk or shooting guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has anyone alleged that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I believe that the report that the witness was permitted to read described that as Mr. Milankovic and his group of people. So I just want to find out if this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time did you ever see Mr. Milankovic drunk or shooting guns?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. Neither did I see him drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And at any time in your experience, did you ever see people who you recognised as Milankovic's men, perhaps by their uniform or in his presence, who were drunk or shooting guns? Did you ever personally see that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them shooting but I did see Tito Potok drunk. He was drunk. And he set on fire the house of Ifet, and then he said: Look at what the green berets have done to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, I must have confused you. I'm -- in your entire life experience, have you ever seen people aside from Tito Potok who may have been a Wolf of Vucjak? Have you ever seen Milankovic's men so that you could identify them as his men, drunk and shooting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think you confused him. He answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'll fix that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tito Potok, he was the man who asked you to fix the -- hot wire the Mercedes, right? At the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't ask me to. He said: "You have to start the Mercedes. You have to start the engine." And then I said to him that I would look around to see if I could find somebody who knew how to hot wire the car. I went around, wasn't able to find anybody, and then he started looking for me in order to kill me. I heard that from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You told us the story already. It was a very simple question. You were asked to identify this man as the one you had referred to before with regard to the Mercedes, that's it. You should have answered just yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could listen to my question, that's the information I'm really looking for. This man Tito Potok, was he wearing a Wolves of Vucjak insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you knew him from before that day, because you knew his name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so that night you didn't know his name? And someone told you later who he was?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it himself, as he was sitting by the fire, that his name was Tito Potok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this man, that night, and that day that you were at the sawmill, this particular man was drunk, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think in response to Mr. Nicholls' question, I think you said that Mr. Milankovic's men had set up checkpoints in 1991. Was -- was that near his village of Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had they done it not as a member of the armed forces, not as a member of the police, but just as a paramilitary group, a group of men who got together to play soldier, they set up their own checkpoint? Is that how you meant it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they set up checkpoints, one couldn't pass through, everybody's identity was checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That checkpoint that you know about, that was the one near Vucjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be correct then also that you don't know of any other checkpoints that particularly Mr. Milankovic's men set up? Would that be correct too?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the other checkpoints. I just know that there were checkpoints around our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the checkpoints around your village, didn't your TO unit set up such a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your unit set it up and you never participated in that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, it was the Serbs who held that checkpoint, when Lisnja was set on fire. At that time, we couldn't pass through if we didn't have our IDs on us, regardless of the fact that they knew who we were but they still wouldn't let us through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because I'm convinced that in your statement, which you have in front of you, that there -- you said in your statement that your TO unit was -- had set up and manned a checkpoint also, previous to the sawmill incident. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can she refer him to the part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thought she was referring to his written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it yesterday and just a couple of minutes ago he said something to that effect too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that your TO unit, when you were a member of it, did that as well?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I went and patrolled along the road. We had patrols in the village, and I know that there was a checkpoint there but that was when Lisnja was torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how about on page -- in the English, it's on page 3, and it's the first, second, third full paragraph down, and I will try and perhaps with Judge Agius's help, we can find where in your statement you talked about before -- before this incident at the sawmill, your TO unit was stopping cars and checking them at the checkpoint by Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to say I don't see that in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think it's on page 3, and the full paragraph down, but there is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not matter what's in the statement, Mr. Mujanic. If your testimony today is that your unit, before the sawmill incident, never detained cars, driving in the area, that's the answer I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a mixed question. She was asking him about his TO unit setting up a checkpoint; that did not appear in his statement. There is nothing I see on the page that he cited about his TO unit setting up a checkpoint. Whether they stopped anybody is a different issue from manning a checkpoint. So I think that needs to be clear for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Nicholls has just stated, you need to take into consideration, Madam Baruch, and rephrase your question accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your written statement it says in English, during 1991, in the village Mravica, the TO stopped a car and recovered weapons and explosives from the trunk. Was that your TO unit?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Territorial Defence was under one command, so we had reports on what was going on in Lisnja, in Mravica, Konjuhovci, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you talked in your statement about 48 people from the TO unit that you were a part of, all were Muslims except for five Serbs, was that your unit?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not the same unit. They were also members of the Territorial Defence but that of Mravica, whereas we were in Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm very concerned because confused. On page 3, in English, and I'll try to find it, it says: "At this time the TO was called up" -- on page 3, the first paragraph -- "Of the 48 people all were Muslims except for five Serbs. The recruiting department of the JNA of Prnjavor sent me an official call-up paper." Was that not to you personally?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before that, in our village, there was a meeting to see -- to select people who were calm, not prone to drinking, and then a list was compiled and it was sent to the military department and then Meho Jasarevic, he signed it, and they issued call-up papers and then the weapons were brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me some idea of the date that that occurred. Was it in 1991 or in 1992, in April?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the weapons, when the weapons were brought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, when the call-up --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the call-up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in 1991. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the first half of 1991 or in the second half? It has been suggested to you that we are talking of April, 1991. If it's 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness corrected me that the machine gun was taken back in April, so it would have to be before April of 1992. Can you give us some idea of when you were called up? Was it the first half or the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the first half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were called up, weapons and two machine guns were distributed, that is, rifles and two machine guns were distributed to your 48-member TO group, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And each of the men received a rifle or firearm. I think you said that they were M48s; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were M48 rifles and two machine guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And each of the members, each of the 48 people who were called up got a gun, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. 46 of them got rifles and then there were two machine guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so two of the people didn't get rifles, those two people got machine guns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you one of the people, Mr. Mujanic, who got a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already stated that. He's confirmed it on more than one occasion. He also said how many bullets, how many rounds he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Because I'm confused a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said in your statement that when it came time for the collection of the gun, you didn't turn in a M48. That's where I got the impression that you also were given a M48 rifle. Was that a wrong thought on my -- that I had?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they came to get machine gun, I was issued a machine gun. And later on, there came about the surrender of M48 rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never had possession of one of those rifles? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're given these weapons in the beginning -- in the first half of 1991, when you're called up, and were you told that your job, as part of this call-up, was to wear your uniforms and patrol the Lisnja area?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were patrolling the area - and I'm not only speaking about you but I'm speaking about your whole unit of the 48 people who were called up - one of the things that you would do would be to stop suspicious cars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or for example people who were drunk, who had weapons, we had to confiscate their weapons to ensure that there was order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to make sure people were not transporting arms, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I bet it's pretty hard to tell from looking at the outside of a car whether or not the person inside it is transporting guns, so would you stop those vehicles that you did not know, that you had no reason to believe should be in the area, and check those cars?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, the vehicles that were not familiar to us, we would stop them, or if we thought that those people whom we knew, such as neighbours, Serbs, Muslims or whoever, might have something in their car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you stopped those cars, the people you didn't know, or the people you had suspicions about, you would ask for their identification, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would ask to inspect the car, the trunk, to see what was in the car, what was being transported, if they had nothing in it we would wish them a safe trip and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never asked them to show you even a driver's licence or some little piece of identification of who they were?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we didn't know them, then yes, we would ask for IDs. If we knew the people, then we wouldn't. In that case, we would simply check the contents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So then yesterday, when you talked about at other checkpoints that only non-Serbs would be stopped at, is there room in your mind, Mr. Mujanic, for the concept that those guards would be stopping and checking the people they did not know? Or had no suspicions about?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the checkpoints at the main road, all vehicles were stopped, suspicious vehicles, people. That's my opinion. We would stop people on the roads. The checkpoints that were outside of Lisnja were manned by Serbs and they would always stop us and ask for our IDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm receiving a transcript on a monitor but not on the laptop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Mujanic, what you saw on the main roads, manned by people you believe were Serbs, is that they would check, they would stop every car and ask every car for their identification; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that personally, when Milankovic and others were stopping people, but that was the normal procedure at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think we understand that you're Bosniak and that that would fall into the classification of non-Serbs. Would it be -- would it then follow, Mr. Mujanic, that what you could personally observe was that when some checkpoint stopped you and that your friends who you've told us were mostly Bosniaks as well, they would tell you that they were stopped at checkpoints but that you don't have any personal knowledge of whether a stranger, unknown to a checkpoint guard who happened to be Serb himself, you don't have any personal knowledge of those -- whether those people were stopped. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but at the time, everybody was stopped, regardless of who they were at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you say "at that time," I assume that you're referring the Court to 1991, all the way through 1992, before the sawmill incident. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then later on it was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, after the sawmill, pretty close in time to that, you were in Sloga for more than a month, right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, and it might have been a translation error, when you were telling the Court about the TO unit, the one that you were called up in, my translation said that there were 40 members. But when I looked at your written statement, I saw that you had written 48 members. When you wrote it, you were correct, or when you signed the written statement, it was 48 members, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know the exact number myself but it was between 40 and 48.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling us today is even when you said the 40 members you didn't know the exact number. When you said -- when you signed the statement that said 48 members, you didn't know the exact number. Both of them were guesses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't guessing. I know that it was about 40, 40 something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason that I ask you that is I think there is pretty big difference between a unit that has 48 people, five of which are Serbs, and 40, five of which were Serbs. But we can pass that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you better pass it, Mrs. Baruch, because the Trial Chamber simply doesn't agree with you that there is much difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the five Serbs, one of them is Captain Nedjo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just checked the transcript from yesterday and he didn't say there were exactly 40, he said there were around 40 of us altogether --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think we have been told it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Regardless I want to correct words she was putting in his mouth from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, the five Serb members, one of those five was Captain Nedjo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't count them and he was separate, he was for the Muslim part of Lisnja and the settlement of Lisnja but there were some TO members on the main road as well, in the village alone there were 40 or 48 of us, together with those five Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then the other five Serbs, they were just TO members, just of the same rank as you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the same place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were Muslims, at least n 1991, who were even -- who even had more authority than Captain Nedjo. For example, in your statement, you told us that the call-up order came from Banja Luka, from a Muslim named Meho Jasarevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The mobilisation was for the TO, and when we were supposed to go to Croatia, that's when the order came. Captain Nedjo showed us a paper and said: "This has just arrived from Banja Luka. We have to go at least for a day to look to see what it's like at the battlefield."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you refused to go?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. I just want to correct something for the record. The statement does not say that Meho Jasarevic was from Banja Luka. It says he was from Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it your entire TO unit then or just you that refused that mobilisation, Mr. Mujanic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the mobilisation. We refused to carry out the order to go across the Sava River to the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But other than that, as a TO member, you followed the orders that you were given?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. But we didn't want to go and wage the war, and shoot at people, regardless of who those people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you got that mobilisation order, then, did that mean that you were a full-time TO officer or member? Full time, that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my full time obligation, to be in the village, and we did not want to move anywhere outside the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you corrected me before and said that there were 46 M48 rifles. I need to ask you something about the rifles because yesterday you said, I think, that half of them didn't work, and I think in your statement you said something like seven or eight didn't work. Can you tell me if, when it was working, that was a good rifle? If it worked? It was one that could shoot bullets and you could be used -- could be used for defence or whatever one would use a rifle for?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rifles were not in the proper working order. They couldn't be cocked up and on one occasion, we had a target practice on Pavlovo Brdo. We were supposed to fire three bullets into the target but we couldn't because they were out of order and there was a promise that they would be fixed but it never happened. When we were in our -- in the culture centre, that was our headquarters, that's where we kept all those rifles that were out of order and those who had to stand guard, those who were doing shifts, they were the ones who were given those very few rifles that were in a good working condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 3 of your statement, in Serbo -- in B/C/S, the third paragraph down, I think that last sentence, which I'll probably murder your language in, says [B/C/S spoken]. Does that mean seven or eight didn't work?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if 46 rifles are given out, we have about 39 that according to your statement were working, with about 48 men in the TO unit. I count that as a pretty formidable force. Do you not think that that many men, with those many guns, would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Baruch, you seem to forget most of the time that there is no lay jury in this trial. We are all professional judges and we are not impressed by questions like the one you have just put.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps the witness can help me understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that one night there was some shooting in the air and that people were singing songs and you did not go to investigate. Were you there that night?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a patrol, and I did hear the singing and the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big is a patrol, please?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And none of the four of you went to investigate that matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell from the voices about how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not have guessed that. But in any case, I heard several voices singing; how many, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also said something about one time your TO unit arrested a Bosniak soldier who was shooting up in the air. Did you do that or was it one of your compatriots, your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That includes you personally, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, when Mr. Nicholls was questioning you, about military trucks that were on the main road between Banja and Prnjavor, filled with ammunition that were probably Serbian army trucks. Did you know who was in that trucks actually? Did you have actual knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't tell you exactly, but I know it was the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that from the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would it also be correct that you did not know what they were carrying in those trucks that were driving on the roads?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that could have been on the trucks was ammunition, because it was escorted by the troops and by helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So because you saw military trucks with troops and helicopters overhead, you made that assumption, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other trucks behind which were not covered, and I did see boxes like the ones that are used for the transport of weapons and ammunition. That's how I concluded that all of the cargo was ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see anybody shooting from those trucks?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, but I heard from the people who lived by that road, and I also saw that some windows were broken, and I also saw bullet holes on some of the walls of those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn now to your statements about the turning in of weapons in Lisnja. Yesterday when you were testifying, and also this morning, you spoke without giving any dates of the turning in of weapons. In your statement, you indicated, I think, that in April was when Captain Nedjo came and asked for the machine gun from you, April of 1992. Does that sound correct to you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I returned my machine gun to Captain Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was before what you described in your statement as a written order to turn -- to surrender weapons to the police in Prnjavor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was before that that I surrendered my machine gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from reading your statement, although it's hard, and I have to do a lot of guessing, I think it was in May of 1992 that -- maybe in the middle of May of 1992, that you heard about the first order which you described as a written order to turn in weapons to the police station in Prnjavor. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I take it Madam Baruch, that you are referring to the last paragraph on page 3 of the written version of his statement, and that is limited to hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was in May of 1992, and in fact, it does say that. It says in the beginning of May 1992, there was a written order. Did you ever see that written order?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it. It lasted for two or three days, and we wanted these hunting rifles to be collected as soon as possible, handed over as soon as possible, so as to avoid any possible problems. That's what we decided to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say it lasted about two or three days, the order as you understood it, required hunting rifles to be turned in within three days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although you didn't see it, this order was communicated to you. Who communicated that order to you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enver Gvozdjar and other people attended the meeting at which it was said that all the hunting rifles should be turned over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been a large meeting of the people or maybe only the men from the village of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a meeting in the restaurant called Europa. And that's where the meeting was attended also by a security captain, our representatives were there, and this is the place where it was agreed that the weapons should be handed over. This is the information that we received, and according to that information, whoever had hunting rifles were supposed to hand it over and take it to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you said Europa. I just -- the only reason I need the name of the place is I'm trying to find out if you were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's already said a couple of times that he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think he said he didn't read the written order; it was conveyed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he referred to this yesterday too. Give us your answer, please. Were you present at this meeting in the Europa restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So somebody gave that information to the people at the restaurant and then somebody from the restaurant transmitted that information to the other people in Lisnja. Who told you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirso Kobaslija, Enver Gvozdjar -- Enver Gvozdjar is also a hunter and he was the one who communicated the information to other hunters. I also received that information, somebody -- I was told that because I had my brother-in-law's hunting rifle, so I also handed that over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so as this information trickled down to you through those people, you were told all hunting rifles had to be turned in so you took your brother-in-law's guns. And by the third day, as communicated to you, you brought that gun -- those guns, I think you said two of them, to Prnjavor. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be correct that I did take them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you confirm the information with your captain from the TO so that at least you had some information that it was a reliable direction to bring the guns there? Did you confirm that with Nedjo?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But we had our representatives, Enver Gvozdjar and Mirso Kobaslija, who communicated the information to us. Obviously we trusted that information, given to us by our people and we took the weapons where we were supposed to take them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm assuming, tell me if you know I'm wrong, that over that three day period, people would go when it was convenient for them to turn in these rifles, these hunting rifles; is that right? You happened to go on the third day.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all of us got together, got into a truck, collected the weapons, and handed them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of those people went to Prnjavor, actually themselves, then? See what I'm trying to find out is whether you as a group of representatives collected all of the hunting rifles and brought them to Prnjavor or each person collected their own and went themselves.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person, each hunter, everybody who had a licence, was supposed to hand over their own weapons, because they were issued with a receipt for the weapons that was handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. When you went that day to Prnjavor, did you go in your TO uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went with a bunch of -- with several other people. Were there a lot of people there when you were turning in the hunting rifles of your brother-in-law or your brother?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were troops there with the SAO Krajina insignia. There were also policemen there. They lined us up in a single file. They instructed us to go into a room where we handed over the weapon. We were issued with a receipt. And then they would -- then we would go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This SAO Krajina, is that a place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that it was on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw some troops there in that uniform with the SAO Krajina thing who were hassling you or making comments to you, but they didn't hurt anybody, did they?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't hurt anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there one truck of such troops or more than one truck?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many men, please?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than ten?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could have been as many as 50?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't tell you that with 100 per cent certainty. I know there were quite a number of them but as to their exact number, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on the first day maybe you said you went with a group of 30 people. So would it be correct that there were about 30 people from Lisnja there when you were there turning in the guns?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People came from the entire Prnjavor municipality. All of them Muslims. And they all brought their weapons. They were aware of the request to hand over their weapons. They all did that to avoid any possible problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the information to turn in the gun was communicated to you by a Muslim representative; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So wouldn't you have expected that the other people from around Prnjavor would have been given that information from their Muslim representatives to turn it in within three days?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they also received that same information. There were quite a few people there who were all turning in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any Serbs with regard to orders from their Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not talk to any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then in your statement it says: "About three or four days later, your SDA representative told you that any hidden weapons had could be collected by noon and would be collected by the military." That's true, right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason I just referred you to that, because reading from page 4 of your original statement, you wrote: "This same day, two groups of Muslim men, about 10 to 15 in each group, refused to hand over their weapons, they were telling everyone if they surrendered the weapons, the Muslims would all be killed, and during this incident, Captain Nedjo was present. These two groups ordered Captain Nedjo, two aids, and three Muslims against the wall and took the surrendered weapons. Then they left the village and went to a hill called Vinogradine." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason that I gave that preliminary statement from the paragraph before that about three or four days later, after you had turned in the hunting rifles, the representative told you hidden weapons would be collected by noon by the military. Was it that three or four days later, after you turned in your hunting -- your brother-in-law's hunting rifles, that this incident occurred with these 30 young Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pekic came. He was the SDA president. He was the one who told us that all the weapons should be handed over by noon. And people did that, whoever had anything, they brought it and handed it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those weapons, those were not the hunting rifles that you were told about in the first order. These were any other kinds of privately owned gun; is that right? I think you used the word "automatic weapons" even. So these were different guns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that day, before noon, is it correct, a lot of people came in and turned in their private weapons, the ones you described as automatic weapons? Is that true? A lot of peaceful citizens did that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They turned it in to whom, to the military forces?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Nedjo was there, and two other soldiers. There were our representatives there as well. That is in the local commune. And it was recorded what weapons were handed in. Then guys came, collected the weapons, without any ammunition, and left for Vinogradine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where that was, where that took place?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the Carsija, in the local commune headquarters, which was also part of the culture centre, so it was all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like if somebody used the term Dom Kulture, that's the area that it was collected at? That those guns were collected at?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Dom Kulture, the local commune headquarters and its office is next door to the Dom Kulture. It's all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have any weapons to turn in on that occasion three or four days after you turned in your brother-in-law's weapons or brother's weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what I'm really trying to figure out, then, Mr. Mujanic: Were you there when that happened? Were you at the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By the Dom Kulture, there is a restaurant or a coffee place, and I was standing on its terrace with a number of other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were watching from a distance away, not too far a distance but you were watching from a distance away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was some 10 or 15 metres away from that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know each and every one of those 20 to 30 young men who took the guns?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know every one of them. I actually knew just one of them, whose family name is Katanic and his first name is Edin. That's the only guy I really knew. As or the others, I just sort of knew them by sight. I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is no way to tell if a gun is loaded unless you open the gun and look in it. Would we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An automatic weapon has to have a clip with ammunition. I didn't see any clips on those automatic weapons. That's how I knew that the guns were not loaded. They were not filled with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the guns that were turned in by the people from Lisnja? Those guns?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Captain Nedjo carried a gun, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Nedjo had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's start being to escape me. He has explained his basis for thinking that these rifles were not loaded. I just don't know where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The objection sustained, yes. Proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 20 to 30 men that came and took these automatic weapons and private weapons from Nedjo and his two aides and the three Muslims reported on your statement, those men carried guns as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims did not carry guns. The only person who had any weapons was Captain Nedjo. I saw that. I don't know about the others. I didn't see them carrying anything. Maybe they had pistols and nobody approached these soldiers anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers? What soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who arrived together with Captain Nedjo. I did not see any weapons on them. I see a weapon that is an automatic rifle on Captain Nedjo but not on the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Nedjo was there with some soldiers, and this group of 20 to 30 men who are Bosniaks, go there and take against orders, the orders being to turn in the guns, they took the guns from at least one person who was armed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Captain Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think some place you described a hundred hunting weapons plus other weapons. Do you know what -- how many weapons were taken on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't know. I believe that we had about 100 hunting snipers. There were a lot of hunters in the village. And that is what I know for a fact. As for the rest, I can't give you the exact number. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the exact number. I'm sure the Court would be interested in knowing about how many guns these young men took from Captain Nedjo, who was armed. Could you see that? And if you couldn't, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the rifle was taken from Captain Nedjo because I saw a man carrying an automatic rifle with a clip, and as for the others, without the ammunition, I don't know how many were taken. People had maybe one rifle each. Nobody had two rifles. So I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw these young men take rifles as well as automatic weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rifles were what people surrendered, and the automatic weapons were surrendered. So all of that together was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the other thing that confused me about this when I was reading your statement and listening to your testimony is: I couldn't tell if that incident occurred on the same day that Mr. Milankovic announced on a megaphone that everybody from the village had to leave and go to the sawmill. Can you tell me if this incident was on that same day?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it would be correct, wouldn't it, that after the guns were taken by the men who went towards a hill called Vinogradine, that is, when the announcement was made that everybody should come out of Lisnja and go to the sawmill, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how long after that incident were you at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, I just need -- the Court Reporter said to me he couldn't get the spelling of the German town in which you gave the statement to the police. Could you spell that for us.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kirhajm Tek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the letters?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: K-i-r-h-a-j-m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the complete name of the town?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kirhajm Tek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to look at your Serbian statement on page 5, the paragraph before the end, I'll read you the sentence that I think is important. You tell me if that was gotten down correctly. When you gave your statement, on page 5, in B/C/S, the paragraph before the end statement, the second sentence: "[B/C/S spoken]." I think that says, at least it's translated in English, that you did not see the young men that the Hodza went to get because they were put on trucks to go to Prnjavor. Did you say that to the investigator who came to speak with you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I probably got confused somewhere. Because they were taken in trucks, but I got confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that when you said back in 2001, a time closer to the incident, that you did not see those young men, those men, you were confused?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see the young men as they were coming down, two young men, a father and a son, and they were the ones who were beaten. As they were walking down, they were beaten with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so those were the two men that you saw coming out of Lisnja, throwing down their weapons, those two people?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't see everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And those two people who you saw coming out, those two people who threw out their weapons, they are coming out after the shelling started, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling had already started when they were walking down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement that you gave back in 2001, you told the Prosecutor that you saw the shelling, that there were four shells, three from a rocket launcher and one from a recoilless. That's on page 5 of your statement. Is that correct? That's what you saw as the shelling.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shells were landing there. One landed near the mosque and one landed on my brother-in-law's barn and that's how it was torched. When we get there, after -- when we got there after we were released, we were able to see the consequences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You just said that you saw two shellings, one of the barn and one of the mosque. Did you also see two other shellings but you didn't see, couldn't see, where they landed?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of shells fired. I can't tell you exactly how many because the noise was quite substantial as the multiple rocket launcher fires them quite noisily but I can tell you that there were a number of shells that were fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't see where the other shells landed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you also -- and I don't even know if you would be able to hear -- but did you also hear bullets from guns at any time while you were up at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard the firing. Once the army started from the place where we were. We could hear the firing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the armed men from your position, the Wolves of Vucjak, then, as infantry or as Milankovic's army, then after the shelling, the major shelling, they walked to the town which was higher up a hill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see them actually get to the village and go into the village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That village is the village of Puraci, and it was some 20 metres from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the village or hamlet of Lisnja? Did you see them get to Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of that is called Lisnja, Puraci and Lisnja are together. Puraci is a separate hamlet, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you said the people left Lisnja, did you mean that people from Puraci left and went to the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from Puraci. People came from Puraci. Now, I couldn't tell you anything more detailed because that was to the right of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you were standing, I'm understanding that Puraci was quite close to where you were at the sawmill but you also said your brother-in-law's barn was set on fire. Is your brother-in-law's barn actually in Puraci or is it in the village or hamlet of Lisnja? And explain it to me, if I just confused you.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barn is in Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from where you were standing and you're looking up the hill, first one would see Puraci and then beyond that would be Lisnja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you could easily see Puraci but did -- and I think you've told me you also could see the soldiers from the sawmill actually walk into the village of Lisnja or the hamlet area, at which your brother's barn was or brother-in-law's barn.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is just a road dividing and leading to Lisnja. Puraci on the right and if you continue straight, you would get to Lisnja. So Puraci hamlet is to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining that. And as these soldiers actually got to the centre of the Lisnja part, did you hear shooting of bullets?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there much shooting?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that much. It lasted for half an hour perhaps. But it wasn't very intense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't dare ask you how many shots you heard but it was nice of you to help us by giving us a time. Would you agree with me that from the distance you were away and the place where the soldiers went into and the fact that there were buildings and roads in Lisnja centre, that you couldn't tell what direction the bullets were being fired from?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could tell that because we could hear the shooting quite near. It was dusk, so we could see the fire, the sparks, from where the bullets were fired, and there were just elderly there and the people that had returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were not in that village yourself; isn't that true? You were at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, after you got to the sawmill, when you say everybody had left Lisnja except the elderly and infirm, in fact, those 20 or 30 men were still in the area towards the town of Lisnja, isn't that correct, up the hill?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but as Hodza left, other people started pouring in. I didn't see all of these people but that's what I heard later, that all of them had come down, that all of them had returned, and were transferred to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that clears it up a little bit. You didn't actually see this. This is what somebody else told you afterwards, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw only the two men who had thrown away their weapons and who were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also know, don't you, that at least one person was still in the Lisnja area up in a tree, Osman Rahimic, who did not surrender on that day that you were at the sawmill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ask him first whether he's heard of the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought we went over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Osman Rahimic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't this witness. It was another witness, Madam Baruch, that told us about the person you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That he was in the wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Osman Rahimic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you mention him with regard to looting and having seen civilians looting houses?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you know at least one person who did not surrender and come out of the town, who was not elderly or infirm, who remained in Lisnja during this whole incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he ever said he wasn't elderly or infirm. He said there was one person who observed looting from a tree. For whatever relevance that's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree Osman Rahimic was not an elderly or infirm person?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. He was 40 something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you later get to speak with Osman Rahimic, didn't you, about the incidents on that day?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came and joined us in the camp. He had surrendered, reported to the police, and came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Sloga, right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Didn't he also tell you that he was armed when he was hiding in the woods around Lisnja? And he turned in his gun as well as himself? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. He didn't tell me that he had had a weapon, nor do I know of that. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Did he tell you that there were other men hiding in the woods along with him?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had been alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had some kind of a contact in the village of Lisnja who was giving him information about what was going on? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about that. He just saw when the village was torched. He saw soldiers and officers looting and carrying away property items and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also said "and civilians"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in a casual conversation at Sloga, when he was giving his story to you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told that to us, not just to me alone. There were other people there. We asked him what happened to him, he had stayed behind and nobody knew what was going on with him for some 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be correct, Mr. Mujanic, that you don't really know whether or not there were people hiding in Lisnja before the soldiers with Milankovic actually entered the village of Lisnja? Would that be correct? If somebody was hiding, you wouldn't have known?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. So I can't say anything different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you agreed with me, but I'm not sure. You don't know, nobody brought to your attention, whether or not somebody was hiding in Lisnja at the time that the soldiers went in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as we learned later on, there was nobody except for Osman Rahimic hiding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you certainly heard shots being fired from several directions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were encircled from all sides, Lisnja was, and after we came back, there was shooting from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.
