So what you're telling this Tribunal, I think, is that you attribute any bullets that were coming from a different direction than the direction of Milankovic's men, you attribute that to, for example, the troops from Laktasi who you said were on the other side of the village? Is that what you're trying to indicate?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting from all sides. I can't say that it was only Milankovic's people shooting because everybody else was shooting, and the area that they passed through is the area where houses were torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you attribute --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Milankovic's people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attribute, if there was any shooting at Milankovic's people or at soldiers coming from the direction you were at, you attribute that to the two groups of soldiers shooting at -- towards each other as they were entering the village from all sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think that's a fair characterisation of what he's been saying. He didn't say anybody was shooting at Milankovic's men. And there is two -- she's kind of mixing two different times. When he was at the sawmill she as asking him about shooting, as the Milankovic's troops went into Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may be right, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now he's talking about afterwards when the town was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may be right and probably he is. I'll give you an opportunity to rephrase your question or to put more than one question along the lines that has been suggested to make sure that we are not confusing two separate timeframes here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk about as the soldiers entered the main village of Lisnja, Mr. Mujanic. Are you saying that there was no return fire against the soldiers from Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that had a fire been opened, had somebody been injured, we would have been all killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's given you an answer too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that all the information you know about that? Because I'm trying to find out if your statement was that there was nobody resisting Milankovic's men as they went up the hill and into Lisnja. Would you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as it was dark, they stationed themselves in various houses. For example, they would start fire in the middle of a living-room, have barbecue. I learned that from a relative of mine because they were in his house, they set up fire in his living-room, and were sitting there drinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not confuse -- I mean, you're not answering the question. The question is a very simple and direct one. Mrs. Baruch wants to know whether you are in a position to confirm that there was or there wasn't any kind of armed resistance or firing back from the town of Lisnja or from the hamlet of Lisnja on Milankovic's troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you're confirming that there was no fire coming from that direction, from the town of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps you can tell us how you know that, whether you know it from your own observations or whether it's because you have been told that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from the others that there was nobody left there with weapons who could have been able to shoot at Milankovic's men, and we also knew it because had a fire been opened then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You have told us that. Now, Mrs. Baruch, he's back in your hands, perhaps you can ask him the next question that Mr. Nicholls maintained could be confusing as to the two different timeframes, if you want to proceed with that question. But we have at least one explanation for sure, and that is that when Milankovic's name -- troops entered the men of Lisnja, approached the town of Lisnja, there was no resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What you know is that none of Milankovic's men were injured; is that correct? To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Because the other day you talked about one person, Sead, I think his name was, who had a shotgun shell in his arm. How did that happen? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't Senad. It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdic. It was Avdic. I can't remember his first name. He had a shotgun wound in this area. He was all bloodied and he was coming from Puraci area. We saw, as they beat him with rifle butts and all other kinds of implements and he held his arms above his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw this person, Avdic, coming out of the Puraci area with --

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Senad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was after the shooting had started, after the shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did I see that right? Did you say that he was -- if you look at me, that he was injured in this area, like by his back?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here. It went through the muscle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is indicating the muscle between -- over the scapula, connecting the scapula and the neck, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Senad Avdic, did you see him also turn in a gun?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you didn't see him shoot himself either, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to suggest that he was shooting himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was shot before he was coming down from the hill. As he was coming down from the hill his hands were up and some soldiers were taking him into custody and hitting him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. As they were taking him into custody and walking with him on the road, I could see that this area here was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the next morning, they brought him to the hospital, correct, or towards Prnjavor -- before everybody else, right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That very night, they took him to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, my paper got changed. The fighting, did it go on -- or the shooting, did it go on through the night or was it only until you saw the soldiers get into the village of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At dusk time, everything stopped, and they went into houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all of this activity that involved shelling or shooting, it was sometime between the afternoon, I think you said 1600 is when the shelling started, to dusk; would that be correct, Mr. Mujanic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it start up again the next morning?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, we could hear a bullet here and there, only occasionally, but there wasn't much firing. However, we could see the smoke rising, smoke plumes from the houses, barns and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you heard occasional bullets but the fires were still at least smouldering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smouldering, yes, and some had been set on fire just a few hours before that when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were actually in the village of Lisnja, did you observe anybody start a building on fire?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were returning to the village, there were houses that were on fire, and there were houses that were smouldering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what you saw. But you didn't observe any particular person set any house on fire, right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally saw a man leaving my house that he had set on fire. It was already burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your village?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By sight from where?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was from Ilova, but at any rate, we were together in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You confused me yesterday when you talked about mopping up stage -- you talked about mopping up but the people from the village of Lisnja were not there. What do you consider mopping up?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was mopping up, but the soldiers had passed through and they wouldn't let us return into the village until the troops had left it. So we were released a little bit earlier so we were able to see the soldiers still in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer you better to a report that Mr. Nicholls showed you, that was dated June 3rd of 1992, and he read to you from the last sentence of paragraph 2, which stated, "Measures have been taken to continue mopping up the areas of Kozarac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Lisnja, a village near Prnjavor." And Mr. Nicholls asked you if you agreed with that report from Exhibit -- I think it was on P659, that there was mopping up, and you said: "Yes, there was mopping up but we were not there." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no people there. One group came by a tractor in the morning, and they picked up all the infirm and the disabled and elderly, so there was nobody else there but that guy Inic [phoen] who was hiding somewhere in the fields. The village was deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was being mopped up? You mean when you say mopping up, that the elderly and infirm were taken out of the village? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I meant was -- when I gave my statement, is that Kljuc and Lisnja and Kozarac were being mopped up. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Baruch, one moment. Throughout this year and a half that we've been holding this trial, we have had several instances where we had to go through this question of what's the meaning of mopping up. And as Mr. Ackerman can confirm to you, we have different interpretation and different meanings given to the term mopping up, depending on the context in which the word is used and also who is using it. There seems to be a military significance to the term mopping up, when used particularly in military documents. There is a health or sanitary significance to the term when it's being used in civilian terms. And there are also other explanations that have been forthcoming from time to time. So we must first, before you can proceed with further questions on this mopping up matter, make sure that the sense in which it is used in the military document that he has been referred to is the same that he intends. Because otherwise, you would be talking at cross-purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Mujanic, can you tell me what you mean when you say -- use the word "mopping up"?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't use the word mopping up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: He agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's someone else that who has used the term. This is what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he was -- I'm trying to explain. He was told yesterday, he was read out this paragraph, from document Exhibit P659, the paragraph 2, which states; "measures have been taken to continue mopping up the areas of Kozarac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc and Lisnja, a village near Prnjavor." So the question -- first question should be: What do you understand by the term "mopping up" the areas of Kozarac, as it appears in this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we follow up with the next question: Would you agree that that was taking place, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's what I was really trying to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, what did you understand by that term, "mopping up"?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mopping up is when the army is in the village and if resistance had been put up, then the infantry comes in and mops up the area. That's what I mean when somebody says mopping up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said then the infantry comes in and mops up the area. So can you tell me what you mean in that -- how you understand that concept.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is the army, then the army penetrates an area, moves forward, and that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please, could you give the witness the B/C/S version of this document? It's -- if you don't have it readily available, I can give you mine. I think that's quicker. Here. And refer him to this paragraph 2, here, and he explains to us the last two and a half lines, whether this is what he means when reading that document. It means that the infantry steps in to clear up the mess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you were to explain it in your own words, how would you express yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mopping up involves infantry, there was some resistance put up, and the infantry comes in to mop up the enemy in order to be able to move forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is that how you understood what was done on that day -- day and the next morning, as the infantry walked into Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way I understood it. I understood it as if there was mopping-up operation through Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the next day, the next morning, they didn't take you to Prnjavor, you went to another village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed with relatives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We escaped, we heard shooting around the village. My neighbour woke me up and then we went to Konjuhovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Konjuhovci. When you went to Konjuhovci?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Konjuhovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said we escaped and we went there. And who did you stay with at Konjuhovci?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hodza, Jusuf accommodated us there. He told us where to go because he knew the people who were willing to receive the people. So he was the one who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you used the word hiding, that you escaped and you went there to hide. Is that the correct connotation?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then. If that's what I said, then that's what I said. We went there to escape any negative consequences. We didn't want anything to happen to us. That's why we fled to Konjuhovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there came a time when you left Konjuhovci and went back to Lisnja too, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you do that? Why did you go back to Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a house there. I had livestock there. There was nobody there to look after all that. I had to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of your relatives in Germany at that time, Mr. Mujanic, or did you have some relatives that were still in the Prnjavor area?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not my close relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you said yes, you mean yes, I did have some relatives, not close relatives, who were in the Prnjavor area, that's my understanding. Did you also have access to some money? Did you have money in the Prnjavor area?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had some very little money, not much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess the reason that I'm asking you is because you said that you gave -- you left Sloga by perhaps bribing an inspector, first on credit but then you returned and did pay him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, on the following day I had borrowed some money from the brother's Mujanics, they had a lot of money they had about 50.000 German marks. I had borrowed money from them to be able to pay this guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, when you left the area of Prnjavor, I think that you paid the bus driver some money as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said 1.600 deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that your money as well?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife sent that money from Germany, and she sent it on that same bus that I would later take to go to Germany. She sent me about 2500 German marks. It was the money that she raised together with my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after you went back to Lisnja, you were told that you were going to be put, detained at the Sloga factory, and you peacefully went to Sloga. I understood that correctly, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not what he said on direct at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you refresh my recollection? Were you arrested and taken to Sloga?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meho Mujanic was told that we had to surrender, some 30 of us took a tractor, went to Prnjavor, surrendered there, we came to the police station, and we were kept there. We were interrogated. And then we were taken by buses to the Sloga shoe factory under the police escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a part of the factory that was not in use? Clearly it must have been.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That factory had been used before, and there used to be a machinery on the production floors but that machinery had been taken in an unknown direction. I don't know where it was taken to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then once you got to Sloga, every day at about 10.00 or most every day, unless there was unusual circumstances, the friends and relations of people who were detained in Sloga were permitted to bring food, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were permitted, if they had some, to bring clothing or bedding as well, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see anybody who brought -- had clothing brought to them or bedding?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I was in the other room. And I didn't see anybody with bedding. We all slept either on cardboards or if there wasn't any available, then we slept on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said I was in the other room. Do you have reason to believe that the people in the other room had access to bedding and clothing if they needed it?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. When I was given permission to go to that other room, I didn't see anybody having a mattress or bedding or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to stop here. Madam Baruch, unless you can conclude very, very quickly on this particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I would love to help the Court out and I'm so tired that I couldn't even think straight. And it would go slower if I did it now than if I just do two questions tomorrow. I apologise, Mr. Mujanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I just ask, is that all that's left for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think ten minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm starting an initial appearance and arraignment quite soon for which I have to prepare. So I think we better stop here. Because I have other things to do with my staff before I proceed with the next case. Mr. Mujanic, I'm afraid we haven't finished. You need to come again tomorrow. You will be here only for a few minutes. And after that, you will be free to go back home. We adjourn for today, resuming tomorrow at 9.00 and with the understanding that we will have a morning and afternoon session tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
